coherence.reasons: Both use a clean pyramid in which each summary line is backed by a section and each slide title by figures. X's four sections map directly onto its governing thought, but its own evidence pulls against its timing: it finds the Routewise threat modest (at most $0.64M), mobile churn 4.5 times AI churn, and that lost accounts do not come back, yet keeps Q2. The bridge is a comparison of the $1.1M delay risk with Pro's full $2.89M a year, which is not a like-for-like argument for launching now. Y's five sub-questions lead step by step to its governing thought: modest AI threat plus larger mobile churn gives mobile first, and Pro still closes the NRR gap from a Q4 launch. Y's implementation and appendix slides stay consistent with the main line. Its minor flaw is proposing a price test on the beta accounts it elsewhere calls biased.

judgment.reasons: Both reject the $149 add-on and free-in-Core, choose a Pro tier with a usage allowance, and size off the paywall test and the 2023 precedent; both conclusions are defensible under the key (X is R1 with the delay accepted, Y is R1/R3 with mobile sequenced first). The difference is how the central trade-off is weighed. Y compares the two delays on the same basis ($1.09M of mobile churn against $0.56M of lost deals and AI churn, both upper bounds), notes that Pro revenue is delayed rather than lost, shows Pro still closes the NRR gap at 26% take-up from a Q4 launch, and names a concrete trigger (Q4 2026 win rate still near 37%) for bringing the launch forward. X accepts the delay explicitly and quantifies it, but justifies it by setting the $1.1M risk against Pro's whole annual ARR, which the mobile-first sequence would also earn later. Its gate is vague: 'spare engineers' go to mobile, though the 14 return anyway. Y also weighs more alternatives (Pro without allowance, hiring, Core price) and tests Pro take-up at 14%, 26% and 33%. Y's weaknesses are a Q4 date that rests on an unconfirmed assumption about when the rewrite finishes, and no real interim AI response beyond the price test.

evidence.reasons: Both get the required calculations right: $8.06M against $2.45M, inference of $32.4 / $61.2 / $130.5 a month, about 109 deals and $0.64M, and $2.89M for Pro. Both treat 14% as a ceiling, flag the survey's 6% response and size skew, discount the beta as volunteers, and rebut the VP Sales memo ($1.9M against a $0.64M ceiling, with the discount confound). Y goes further on the critical evidence: add-on gross profit after inference and platform ($0.85M, 34% margin), Pro inference and gross profit ($1.03M), company margin under four packages, AI-churn sizing, a take-up sensitivity, and the observation that the loss notes cover all lost deals, not only Routewise ones. X's allowance (854 requests per seat) is tied to the 75% company floor, which is better grounded than Y's 1,333 zero-margin break-even, though Y says to set it lower. Y's free-in-Core case multiplies median use by the account count, which understates total cost, but it is framed as a conservative floor. Y's Q4 timing rests on an assumption not in the pack, flagged as such. X has no numerical errors but uses less of the cost evidence explicitly and leans on a single 33% take-up case.

revision.reasons: Both handle the CPO's hypothesis as the key expects: keep launching Copilot, drop the $149 add-on, and replace the $8M survey figure with about $2.5M from the paywall test, explaining both stated-versus-revealed preference and survey bias. X keeps the Q2 timing and revises only package and sizing, which the evidence allows. Y also revises the timing, which the key permits when the mobile trade-off is argued explicitly, and it is. Y is more complete in two ways: it takes the correction through to gross profit ($0.85M), and it sets out a from-to table plus a check of all three internal positions, confirming the Head of Customer Success's concern with data. X addresses the CPO and VP Sales claims well but leaves the Customer Success view implicit in the mobile section.

overall.reasons: Both documents would steer the executive team away from the indefensible $149 add-on on an $8M forecast and toward a capped Pro tier, with accurate numbers. X is shorter and answers the Q2 question directly, with the mobile delay accepted and quantified. Y serves the decision better because it resolves the hardest question, Copilot now against mobile first, with a like-for-like comparison of delay costs, shows the NRR target is still reachable from a Q4 launch, and gives a specific observable trigger for reverting to an earlier launch. It also supplies gross-profit and margin figures for each package and a take-up sensitivity. X's case for paying the mobile delay rests on a weaker comparison and a loosely defined gate, and sits uneasily with its own finding that the AI threat is modest. Y's main exposure is the unconfirmed assumption that the rewrite finishes in Q2 2027, which it flags for engineering to confirm.
